result:
None of the three final answers matches my own calculation, but Solution 2 is the closest, so I choose it.

I assumed, as all three solutions do, that the worst case has every person with the same weight vector $a_1,\dots,a_{66}$. I did not prove that assumption.

**Setup.** The selector picks counts $n_j$ with $\sum n_j = 2025$ and gets load $n_j a_j$ on color $j$. A threshold $C$ is feasible for the selector if $\sum_j \lfloor C/a_j \rfloor \ge 2025$.

**Adversary's best weights.** The adversary wants $\sum_j \lfloor C/a_j \rfloor \le 2024$. Write $m_j = \lfloor C/a_j \rfloor$. Then $a_j > C/(m_j+1)$, so $\sum a_j = 1$ requires $C < 1/\sum_j \frac{1}{m_j+1}$. The supremum is therefore $1/\sum_j \frac{1}{m_j+1}$ with $\sum m_j = 2024$.

**Balanced split.** Since $2024 = 66\cdot 30 + 44$, the sum is minimized with 44 colors at $m_j=31$ and 22 colors at $m_j=30$:
$$\sum_j \frac{1}{m_j+1} = \frac{44}{32}+\frac{22}{31} = \frac{2068}{992}.$$
So the supremum is $C = 992/2068 = 248/517 \approx 0.47969$. At exactly this $C$ the selector can afford $m_j+1$ people on each color, so it is feasible.

**Comparing the solutions.**
- Solution 1 gives $31/66 \approx 0.4697$. This is below my lower-bound construction, so it is wrong.
- Solution 3 gives $992/2091 \approx 0.4744$. This is also below the lower bound, so it is wrong.
- Solution 2 gives $992/2069 \approx 0.47946$. This is slightly below $992/2068$ (it looks like an off-by-one error in its integer analysis), but it is the closest and has the right structure.

CHOICE: 2
